lessons.title: Paying for Quality: How Much Premium Is Too Much?

body.text: A moat justifies a premium. It does not justify any premium. The gap between those two sentences is where most of the money lost on great Indian businesses has gone.

children.text: Six chapters have been about identifying moats. This one is about what to pay for them. The two questions are completely separate, and getting the first right while ignoring the second has produced years of flat returns for investors who owned exactly the right companies.
Why a Moat Deserves a Higher Multiple

Two companies can grow earnings at the same rate and still be worth very different multiples, because growth costs them different amounts. A business earning 25% on capital needs to retain far less profit to fund the same growth than one earning 12%. What it does not retain, it can pay out. Value depends on the cash a business can distribute, not the profit it reports.

body.caption: g = sustainable growth rate, ROIC = post-tax return on invested capital, r = cost of equity. The numerator is the share of profit available to shareholders after funding growth.

body.text: Read the numerator carefully. g ÷ ROIC is the fraction of profit that must be reinvested to sustain growth. At 10% growth and 25% ROIC, the company reinvests 40% and can distribute 60%. At 10% growth and 12% ROIC, it must reinvest 83% and can distribute only 17%. Same growth, wildly different cash to shareholders.

children.text: Three Companies, One Cost of Equity of 12%

body.caption: How returns and growth together set a fair multiple

children.text: Companies A and B grow at exactly the same rate, yet A justifies about 30.0 times earnings and B only about 8.3 times. The entire difference is the return on capital, which decides how much growth costs. Company C shows the other half of the story: the same excellent 25% ROIC, but slower growth, justifies about 12.7 times. A moat with no runway is worth much less than a moat with one.

body.title: Calculate a Justified Multiple
body.prompt: A company earns a post-tax ROIC of 20% and can sustainably grow at 8%. Using a 12% cost of equity, what is its justified P/E?
body.explanation: Reinvestment = 8% ÷ 20% = 40%, so 60% of profit is available to shareholders. Justified P/E = 0.60 ÷ (0.12 − 0.08) = 15.0 times. Note how sensitive this is: the denominator is just 4 percentage points, so small changes in growth or cost of equity move the answer a great deal.

children.text: The Premium Has Diminishing Returns

body.title: Justified P/E at 10% Growth and 12% Cost of Equity

children.text: Moving from 12% to 20% ROIC lifts the justified multiple from about 8.3 to 25 times. Moving from 25% to 40% lifts it only from 30.0 to 37.5. Beyond a certain point, extra returns barely matter, because the company is already distributing most of its profit. This is why an extremely high ROCE alone cannot justify a very high multiple. Growth and durability do the heavy lifting once returns are strong.

body.text: This formula assumes the company earns that ROIC and grows at that rate forever, which no business does. It is a thinking tool for comparing companies, not a valuation. Treat its output as an upper bound under generous assumptions, and remember that a growth rate close to the cost of equity produces absurd multiples because the denominator approaches zero.

children.text: Working Backwards: What Is Priced In?

markDefs.definition: Instead of forecasting cash flows to derive a value, you take the market price as given and solve for the growth or returns the price implies, then judge whether those assumptions are reasonable.

children.text: Rather than deciding what a company is worth, it is often more useful to ask what the market is already assuming. Rearranging the same formula gives the growth rate implied by today's price, which is the heart of a
reverse DCF
approach.

body.title: What Growth Is the Market Assuming?
body.prompt: A moat business trades at 60 times earnings. It earns a post-tax ROIC of 25%, and you use a 12% cost of equity. What perpetual growth rate does that price imply, in percent?
body.explanation: Setting 60 = (1 − g ÷ 0.25) ÷ (0.12 − g) and solving gives g ≈ 11.1%. So the price assumes this company grows earnings at about 11% a year forever, while earning 25% on capital forever. That is not impossible for a decade or two, but as a perpetual assumption it is demanding. Your job is to decide whether the moat can plausibly deliver it.

body.label: The question a high multiple asks you
body.value: Not "is this a great business?" but "can it still be great in 2045?"
body.context: At 60 times earnings, most of the value sits beyond year ten, which means you are underwriting moat durability, not next year's results.

body.title: Fade: the assumption that actually matters

children.text: Competitive advantage period
is the number of years a company can keep earning returns above its cost of capital before competition drags them down. Chapters 1 to 6 were, in effect, an extended study of what determines it.

A more realistic valuation assumes high returns for a defined period, then a fade towards the cost of capital. The practical consequence is simple: the multiple you can justify is far more sensitive to how long the moat lasts than to how high returns are today.

A useful discipline is to ask what advantage period the current price implies. If a stock only makes sense assuming 25 years of protected 25% returns, you are making a very long forecast, and the burden of proof from your scorecard should be correspondingly high.
This is also why Section C of the scorecard, durability, deserves more weight than its six points suggest when you are paying a premium multiple.
When a Premium Is and Is Not Deserved

columns.label: A premium worth paying
points: Wide moat with a stable or widening trend
Incremental ROCE at or above reported ROCE
Long runway in an under-penetrated category
Multiple implies growth you can defend with evidence
Management with a good capital allocation record

columns.label: A premium to refuse
points: Growth that comes mostly from price, not volume
Multiple implying perpetual growth near the cost of equity
A single regulatory decision could reset the economics
Story-led rerating with no change in fundamentals
Recent large acquisitions in unrelated industries

children.text: Practical Rules for Indian Quality Stocks
Great businesses rarely get cheap:
waiting for a 15 times multiple on a genuine compounder usually means never owning it. The realistic aim is a fair price, not a bargain.
Buy during deratings, not downgrades:
broad market falls and sector-wide selloffs offer moat businesses at better prices without any change in the moat. A company-specific collapse in fundamentals is different, and needs a rescore first.
Let the scorecard set the multiple:
a 21 out of 24 with a widening trend earns a higher multiple than a 16 with a stable one. Write down the link so you are not improvising under pressure.
Stagger your entry:
buying in tranches over several quarters lowers the cost of being wrong about timing, which matters more at high multiples.
Reassess after a big rerating:
if a stock doubles without earnings following, the moat did not change but your forward return did.

body.title: Which Deserves the Higher Multiple?
body.question: Two companies both earn 24% post-tax ROIC and have wide moats. Company X operates in a category penetrated in over 80% of Indian households and grows 5% a year. Company Y operates in a category under 15% penetrated and grows 14% a year with incremental ROCE of 25%. What follows?
options: Both deserve the same multiple because their moats and returns are equal
Company Y deserves a substantially higher multiple, because the runway lets it reinvest at high returns for far longer
Company X deserves the higher multiple because saturated categories are safer
body.explanation: With ROIC equal, growth and runway decide the multiple. Company X can only distribute cash, which is fine but limits value creation. Company Y can reinvest at 25% for years, compounding value. This is the difference between Company A and Company C in the table above.

body.title: Complete the Principle
body.textWithBlank: The fraction of profit a company must reinvest to sustain its growth equals g divided by ___.
body.explanation: Higher returns mean growth costs less in retained profit, leaving more cash for shareholders and justifying a higher multiple at the same growth rate.

body.title: The 70 Times Decision
body.scenario: A listed Indian consumer company scores 21 of 24 on your moat scorecard with a stable trend. Post-tax ROIC is 28%, earnings have grown 13% a year for a decade, and the category is around 30% penetrated. The stock trades at 70 times earnings after a strong run. Your cost of equity assumption is 12%. A colleague argues that quality always wins over the long run, so the price does not matter.
body.prompt: How would you respond, and what would you actually do?
body.modelAnswer: The colleague is half right. Chapter 1 showed that a moat business bought expensively can still beat a cheap no-moat business over twenty years, because compounding eventually overwhelms a derating. But that argument has two conditions: a genuinely long holding period, and a moat that survives the whole way. At 70 times earnings, the implied perpetual growth using a 12% cost of equity is close to 11%, which requires the company to keep growing at roughly its historical rate essentially forever while sustaining 28% returns. The scorecard says 21 of 24 with a stable, not widening, trend, so the evidence supports durability but not acceleration. Practically: I would not treat this as a binary buy or avoid decision. I would size the position smaller than a similar-quality stock at 40 times, buy in tranches rather than at once, be explicit that my expected return over the next five years is likely below the company's earnings growth because the multiple will probably compress, and set a rescore trigger on the leading indicators from the last lesson. If volumes slow or incremental ROCE falls below reported ROCE, the premium loses its justification and the position should shrink.

body.title: Price a Moat Business
steps: Convert the company's pre-tax ROCE from Screener.in into post-tax ROIC by multiplying by roughly 0.75
Estimate sustainable growth as incremental ROIC multiplied by the reinvestment rate, and sense-check it against the last five years
Calculate the justified P/E using a 12% cost of equity, and treat it as an upper bound
Compare it with the current P/E and note the gap
Work backwards from the current price to the implied growth rate, and ask whether your scorecard supports it
Check how much of the implied value depends on years beyond ten
Set your position size from the gap between the implied assumptions and your evidence, not from conviction alone

body.text: The justified P/E formula assumes perpetual constant growth and returns, which no company achieves. It is a comparison tool, not a valuation model, and is highly sensitive to assumptions. All companies and figures here are hypothetical. Nothing in this lesson is an investment recommendation.

points: Justified P/E = (1 − g ÷ ROIC) ÷ (r − g), because high returns make growth cheaper to fund and leave more cash for shareholders
Two companies growing at the same rate can justify very different multiples purely because of their return on capital
The premium has diminishing returns: beyond roughly 25% ROIC, higher returns add little to the justified multiple
Growth and runway matter as much as returns, so a moat without a runway is worth far less
Work backwards from the price to the implied growth, then ask whether the scorecard supports that assumption
At high multiples you are underwriting how long the moat lasts, not next year's earnings
